Newborn Care

Milk thistle while breastfeeding: evidence and safety

Updated: November 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A product labelled “milk thistle” can mean dried plant material, a concentrated extract or a blend of several herbs. That distinction matters when you are breastfeeding. The useful questions are what was actually studied, whether it helped, and what remains unknown about exposure and safety for your baby.

Milk thistle, silymarin and blessed thistle

Milk thistle is Silybum marianum, a plant with purple flowers. Silymarin is a mixture of constituents extracted from its fruits, often called seeds. A label listing the weight of the whole plant does not describe the same preparation as a measured amount of extract.

Milk thistle and blessed thistle are different plants. Similar common names are not enough to identify a supplement. Check the botanical name, plant part and every ingredient on the label; a breastfeeding claim does not make different products interchangeable.

What the breastfeeding studies actually tested

A 2015 randomized, blinded trial studied a specific micronized silymarin product in 50 mothers who had delivered before 32 weeks. Both groups received feeding support. After 28 days, the product did not improve milk production compared with placebo. The groups differed in starting output and previous breastfeeding experience, which limits interpretation; this was also a small, specific population.

A separate 2016 trial involving 100 mothers of preterm infants reported higher output in the group given a mixture containing silymarin-phosphatidylserine and galega than in the placebo group, according to its published abstract. That result concerns the combined formulation. It cannot tell us that milk thistle alone, a tea or an unrelated capsule will have the same effect.

The practical conclusion is uncertainty. The Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine does not recommend a particular galactagogue routinely on the available evidence. A galactagogue is a substance intended to increase milk production.

Animal results and hormone theories are not a feeding outcome

Claims about milk production in cows or hormone changes in laboratory animals cannot establish a benefit for a breastfeeding family. A proposed hormone or plant-estrogen mechanism also does not show that a baby receives more milk. The relevant outcome is adequate infant intake and growth, with acceptable risks for both parent and child.

What milk testing can and cannot tell us

In the 2015 trial, samples collected on study day 14 had no measurable silymarin above the assay threshold of 0.3 milligrams per kilogram of milk. No important adverse events were reported. A result below a test’s detection limit is not proof that exposure is zero, and a small, short study cannot establish safety for every baby, product or duration.

There is no established “safe breast-milk level” to calculate from that result. If you are already taking a product, show its packaging to your pharmacist or clinician. Discuss the actual ingredients, your baby’s age and health, and any symptoms before deciding how to proceed.

Tea, capsules and food are different preparations

Dried plant material, powders and extracts are distinct preparations. Capsules, softgels, drops and teas may contain different concentrations or additional ingredients. A trial of a standardized extract does not validate a homemade tea recipe, a number of cups per day or a dose copied from a commercial label.

A 2025 study in 16 healthy adults found different absorption with two capsule formulations. Breastfeeding participants were excluded. This illustrates why product design matters; it provides no evidence that an “enhanced absorption” supplement improves milk supply or is safer for a baby.

Traditional food uses of the leaves, buds or seeds are not evidence of a milk-supply treatment. Likewise, a blend with fenugreek, fennel, goat’s rue, marshmallow root or vervain needs assessment as a whole; adding herbs does not resolve the uncertainty about benefit or safety.

Product quality matters, even when the label looks reassuring

NCCIH reports problems with some milk-thistle supplements, including inaccurate silymarin amounts and contamination. A reputable-looking package cannot establish breastfeeding safety. Keep the exact product name, ingredient list and batch details available for a medicine review.

The NHS advises against herbal medicines while breastfeeding because the evidence is insufficient. A traditional-use registration or a long history of use does not by itself demonstrate a reliable clinical benefit. Ask a pharmacist before buying or starting a product rather than trying several formulations in succession.

Allergy and digestive symptoms need attention

Milk thistle can cause digestive upset, including nausea, gas or bloating. Allergic reactions are more likely in people sensitive to related plants such as ragweed, daisies or chrysanthemums. Previous tolerance of a different herbal product does not rule out a reaction.

Stop the supplement and seek advice if a new rash or troublesome digestive symptoms develop. Sudden swelling of the mouth, tongue or throat, difficulty breathing, or fainting can indicate anaphylaxis: call your local emergency number immediately and use a prescribed adrenaline auto-injector if available. Do not wait for a routine appointment.

Check medicines without assuming an interaction is proven

Before combining a supplement with prescribed or non-prescription medicines, ask a pharmacist to review the exact formulation. Mention contraception, seizure medicines such as phenytoin, blood thinners, diabetes treatment, mental-health medicines and cancer treatment. These are reasons for an individual review, not a claim that every combination has a demonstrated harmful interaction.

A laboratory theory about drug-processing enzymes does not establish contraceptive failure in people, and it is not a reason to stop an essential medicine. Keep taking prescribed treatment as directed while obtaining advice. If you have already combined products, give the pharmacist the amounts, timing and any new symptoms.

“Liver detox” claims do not explain breast-milk safety

Claims that milk thistle cleans the liver and releases stored toxins into breast milk are not established by the evidence reviewed here. Equally, taking it cannot be assumed to make alcohol, smoking, medicines or other exposures safe. A concern about a particular exposure needs advice about that exposure itself.

Liver-disease results are inconsistent, and limited studies of blood sugar do not establish a general treatment. Claims about cholesterol, cancer prevention or protection during chemotherapy also should not guide self-treatment. NCCIH emphasizes that little is known about milk thistle’s safety while breastfeeding.

Give feeding concerns a practical assessment

Ask a midwife, lactation professional or clinician to observe a feed and review milk transfer, weight changes and wet nappies. If you express milk, ask about pump fit, technique and a schedule suited to your situation. Longer feeds alone do not prove that more milk is being transferred.

Effective, regular milk removal is central to supporting supply. Medical causes also need attention when appropriate. If your baby needs extra milk, work with the care team on an adequate feeding plan while supporting breastfeeding if you wish; waiting for a supplement to work must not delay needed nutrition.

Know when the baby needs urgent help

Get prompt medical advice if your baby is feeding poorly or has markedly fewer wet nappies, especially with worsening sleepiness or other illness. A baby who is not feeding needs urgent assessment. Call emergency services for breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, marked floppiness, or difficulty waking. These signs should never be managed by changing a parent’s herbal supplement and waiting.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Evidence applies to the products and populations studied; mixed-product results do not isolate the effect of one ingredient.

Limited milk measurements do not establish zero exposure or safety for every infant.

The 2016 mixture trial is summarized from its published abstract; its full report was not available for this review.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to keep your feeding observations and questions together for appointments. It cannot measure milk transfer, diagnose low supply or determine whether a supplement is suitable.

When to seek help

This information does not select a supplement or dose. Feeding problems and possible allergic reactions require appropriate professional care; use emergency services for the severe signs described above.

Evidence notes updated: November 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Milk thistle, silymarin extracts and mixed herbal products are not interchangeable.
  • Studies do not establish a reliable milk-supply benefit or universal infant safety.
  • There is no proven tea recipe or standard self-treatment dose for breastfeeding.
  • A product and medicine review, effective milk removal and adequate infant intake take priority.

Frequently asked questions

What is milk thistle?

It is Silybum marianum. Silymarin is an extract containing several plant constituents; blessed thistle is a different plant. Check the botanical name rather than relying on the word “thistle”.

Does milk thistle increase breast milk?

A reliable benefit has not been established. Results from a particular extract or a blend cannot be applied to every tea or supplement, or to every breastfeeding situation.

How should I make milk-thistle tea for milk supply?

There is no evidence-based therapeutic recipe to recommend. The amount of plant material and extraction vary, and a tea cannot be assumed equivalent to a studied extract. Discuss supply concerns before using it as treatment.

Are capsules safer than tea?

The form alone does not establish safety. Ingredients, concentration, quality, medicines and the baby’s health all matter. Ask a pharmacist to assess the exact product before taking it.

Does “not detected in milk” mean no infant exposure?

No. It means the measurement was below that test’s detection limit. It cannot establish zero exposure or long-term safety.

Can milk thistle detox my milk after alcohol or another exposure?

Do not rely on it for this purpose. Obtain advice about the substance, amount and timing involved; a detox claim cannot establish that breastfeeding exposure is safe.

Should I stop contraception or another medicine while asking about milk thistle?

Do not stop prescribed treatment on the basis of a theoretical interaction. Ask a pharmacist to check the exact supplement and your medicines, and keep taking treatment as directed.

What should I do first if I think my supply is low?

Arrange a feeding assessment that includes your baby’s growth and intake. Get urgent help if your baby is not feeding or seems unwell. Do not delay a recommended feeding plan while trying a herbal product.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
